issues.legal_issue: A restriction prohibiting transfers of property in protected tribal areas to non-tribals, including transfers by non-tribal owners, is a reasonable restriction on the then-existing right to property.
material_facts: The land in the protected areas had originally been occupied by tribal communities, but substantial holdings passed to non-tribals through exploitative lending and trade practices, including transactions that took advantage of tribal owners’ poverty and lack of sophistication.
Earlier protections were circumvented through benami and other clandestine transactions, and tribal owners faced continuing risks of losing their land and livelihood.

The challenged restriction prohibited transfers to non-tribals by both tribal and non-tribal owners; where an owner could not sell to a tribal on acceptable terms, the State was required to acquire the property with compensation.
The challenge was to the restriction’s validity under Article 19(1)(f), as that provision stood at the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: The restriction was constitutionally valid and did not impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) permits reasonable restrictions, assessed objectively in light of the wider community interest and the social conditions the measure addresses. Paragraph 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule empowers regulations restricting land transfers in protected areas. Articles 15(4) and 46 reflect the constitutional concern for advancing Scheduled Tribes and protecting them from social injustice and exploitation. The Court relied on Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka, (1984) 3 SCC 301, and Lingappa Pochanna Appelwar v. State of Maharashtra, (1985) 1 SCC 479, concerning protection of tribal land and restoration of alienated land.

rule.if: constitutional_appeal_challenging_transfer_restriction and tribal_land_was_lost_through_exploitation and earlier_protections_were_circumvented and transfer_ban_covers_nontribal_owners and state_acquisition_is_available_if_no_tribal_buyer

predicates.constitutional_appeal_challenging_transf: A party in a constitutional appeal challenged a restriction on transfers of property in a protected tribal area.
predicates.tribal_land_was_lost_through_exploitatio: Tribal owners lost land through exploitative lending or trade practices benefiting economically stronger outsiders.
predicates.earlier_protections_were_circumvented: People used benami or other clandestine transactions to evade earlier protections for tribal land.
predicates.transfer_ban_covers_nontribal_owners: The restriction also barred non-tribal owners from transferring property to other non-tribals.
predicates.state_acquisition_is_available_if_no_tri: The law provided for state acquisition with compensation when an owner could not sell the property to a tribal buyer on acceptable terms.

issues.definition: When a constitutional appeal challenges a transfer restriction against a background of exploitative loss of tribal land and evasion of earlier protections, and the restriction covers non-tribal owners while providing for state acquisition if no tribal buyer is available, the restriction is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional power to regulate land transfers in protected tribal areas extends to restrictions on transfers of structures fixed to the land.
material_facts: The challenged regulation prohibited transfers of immovable property, including structures on land, in protected tribal areas.
The challenge argued that the constitutional power to regulate land transfers did not extend to structures.
A narrow reading of land would allow the transfer restriction to be evaded by erecting a structure on the land.
issues.conclusion: The expression “land” includes structures raised on it, so the restriction on transfers of immovable property including those structures was within the regulatory power.
issues.legal_principle: Paragraph 5(2)(a) of the Fifth Schedule uses “land” in its comprehensive legal sense, which includes structures fixed to it. The Court referred to The Dictionary of English Law, Words and Phrases Judicially Defined, The Law Lexicon, and Smith v. Richmond, [1899] A.C. 448. A narrow interpretation would undermine the protective purpose of the regulation by making evasion easy.

predicates.constitutional_appeal_challenging_scope_: A party in a constitutional appeal challenged the scope of a regulation governing land transfers in a protected tribal area.
predicates.transfer_restriction_applies_to_property: The regulation restricts transfers of property situated on land.
predicates.attached_structures_are_fixed_to_land: The property at issue includes structures fixed to the land.
predicates.narrow_reading_would_enable_evasion: Excluding structures from the regulated subject would make it possible to evade the transfer restriction by erecting structures on land.

issues.definition: When a constitutional appeal challenges the scope of a land-transfer regulation covering property on land, and the property includes structures fixed to the land whose exclusion would enable evasion, the restriction covers those structures.

issues.legal_issue: A rebuttable presumption that property possessed by a non-tribal person was acquired through a transfer from a tribal person is not unreasonable where the possessor can establish title and tribal owners face proof disadvantages.
material_facts: The regulation presumed that property in a non-tribal person’s possession had been acquired through a transfer from a tribal person, unless the contrary was proved.
The presumption was rebuttable, and evidence of the possessor’s title was a matter the possessor could be expected to disclose.
Tribal owners were often ignorant of their rights and faced substantial difficulties in establishing title to property they had lost.
issues.conclusion: The presumption was reasonable and the challenge to it failed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the reasoning that the presumption was a rebuttable rule of evidence and that, under section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, a fact specially within a person’s knowledge is for that person to prove. The presumption was assessed in light of the practical disadvantages tribal owners faced in proving their rights.

predicates.constitutional_appeal_challenging_owners: A party in a constitutional appeal challenged a presumption about how property in a person’s possession was acquired.
predicates.ownership_presumption_is_rebuttable: The presumption can be displaced by proof to the contrary.
predicates.title_evidence_is_within_possessor_knowl: The possessor can be expected to disclose evidence of the title under which the property is held.
predicates.protected_owners_face_proof_disadvantage: The people whose former ownership is at issue face practical difficulties in establishing their rights.

issues.definition: When a constitutional appeal challenges a rebuttable ownership presumption, the possessor can be expected to know the title evidence, and the protected former owners face proof disadvantages, the presumption is reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge based on the inability to borrow against property fails where a separate provision permits qualifying mortgages without possession.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the transfer restriction prevented a non-tribal owner from raising a loan on the property.
A separate provision permitted mortgages without possession to qualifying financial institutions, subject to conditions.
No appellant claimed to have tried and been unable to raise a loan during the interval before that provision was introduced.
issues.conclusion: The loan-related challenge failed because the separate provision permitted qualifying mortgages without possession, and no actual inability to borrow during the earlier interval was shown.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3A(1), introduced by Regulation 1 of 1971, permitted a mortgage without possession to a cooperative society, bank, or other financial institution approved by the State Government, subject to the applicable conditions. The Court treated that provision as answering the asserted obstacle to raising a loan.

predicates.constitutional_appeal_challenging_transf: A party in a constitutional appeal challenged a restriction on property transfers.
predicates.owner_claims_inability_to_borrow_against: An owner argues that the transfer restriction prevents borrowing against the property.
predicates.qualifying_nonpossessory_mortgage_is_per: The law permits a mortgage without possession to an eligible financial institution, subject to conditions.
predicates.no_actual_failed_loan_attempt_is_shown: The challenger does not show an actual unsuccessful attempt to obtain a loan during any interval before the mortgage permission applied.

issues.definition: When an owner in a constitutional appeal claims that a transfer restriction prevents borrowing, the law permits qualifying mortgages without possession, and no actual failed loan attempt is shown, the loan-access challenge fails.
